question: Y170
answer:
ANSWER

Ask 1 — threshold: 1 EeV (= 10^18 eV = 1000 PeV).
Ask 2 — inclusivity verdict: EXCLUSIVE. The 2024 PDG cosmic-ray review defines UHECRs as cosmic rays with energy strictly greater than 1 EeV ("in excess of 1EeV").

SOURCE AND PROVENANCE

Document: Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics 2024, Chapter 30, "Cosmic Rays (rev.)" — S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024). Chapter revision date printed in the text: 19 September 2024.
File: https://pdgweb.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf, fetched 2026-11-23T21:18:28Z, sha256 c8f0620d58d3.
Chapter identification corroborated by the PDG 2024 Astrophysics & Cosmology contents page (https://pdgweb.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/astro-cosmo.html, sha256 79feac8c9572), which lists "30 Cosmic rays (rev.)" under "2024: Astrophysics & Cosmology".

VERBATIM DEFINITIONAL SENTENCE (Chapter 30, Sec. 30.2, printed page 3 of the chapter)

"CRs with energies in excess of 1EeV are referred to as ultra-high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs)."

VERDICT REASONING

"In excess of 1EeV" is a strict inequality: E > 1 EeV. A cosmic ray of exactly 1.000 EeV is therefore not, by this sentence, a UHECR; the set is open at the lower end. The verdict is read off the review's own wording, not from community convention.

Two nearby usages in the same chapter must NOT be confused with the definition, and are recorded here so a reviewer can check I have not conflated them:
(a) "If CRs with energies in excess of ∼ 1EeV came from sources in the Galactic disk, the angular distribution at Earth would be very anisotropic ..." — this conditional carries a tilde ("∼ 1EeV"). The definitional sentence does not carry the tilde. I therefore report the threshold as the review states it in the definition, exactly 1 EeV, and flag that the tilde appears only in the adjacent physical argument.
(b) "This suggests that there is a transition between the galactic and extragalactic origin of UHECRs around the ankle in the spectrum, at a few EeV." — this is a statement about the spectral ankle and the galactic/extragalactic transition, not about the naming threshold; it is qualitative ("a few EeV") and does not displace the 1 EeV definition.

UNITS, UNCERTAINTY, SAMPLE SIZE

Units: the review states the threshold as "1EeV". 1 EeV = 10^18 eV = 1000 PeV by the definition of the exa-electron-volt prefix (10^18).
Uncertainty: none is quoted. This is a naming convention, not a measured quantity, so no measurement uncertainty applies; the number is given to one significant figure in the review. The absence of a quoted uncertainty is itself a stated property of the source, not an omission on my part.
Sample size: not applicable — the threshold is a definition, not the result of a fit or count. No N is attached to it in the review, and I do not invent one.

CROSS-CHECK WITHIN THE SAME 2024 EDITION (caveat for the reviewer)

PDG 2024 is not internally uniform on this wording. Chapter 36, "Particle Detectors for Non-Accelerator Physics" (rpp2024-rev-particle-detectors-non-accel.pdf, sha256 92b8d56c8743, revised March 2024, Sec. 36.2.1) writes: "An extensive air shower (EAS) is produced by the interactions of ultra high-energy (E > 10^17 eV) subatomic particles in the stratosphere ...", i.e. it uses 10^17 eV as the UHE boundary in a detector-performance context, and separately says UHECRs extend "beyond 10^20 eV". The ask names the *cosmic-ray review*, so the Chapter 30 definition (1 EeV, exclusive) governs the answer. The Chapter 36 usage is a different chapter, a different purpose (shower-production energy for fluorescence detectors), and is not a definition of the UHECR class. A downstream user citing "the PDG 2024 UHECR threshold" should cite Chapter 30 and should not mix the two.

The review gives no separate literature citation attached to the 1 EeV definitional sentence; the definition is the review's own wording. Other thresholds quoted in Chapter 30 are measurement thresholds, not definitions, and are all numerically above 1 EeV, so none of them contradicts the definition: 8 EeV (Pierre Auger large-scale dipolar anisotropy, 6.9 sigma), 38 EeV (Auger CenA excess, 4 sigma), 50 EeV (GZK horizon / fluorescence duty-cycle statements), 57 EeV (Telescope Array hotspot, 2.8 sigma).

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER

If a reviewer consults a different revision of Chapter 30 (the file is dated 19 September 2024, sha256 c8f0620d58d3) and finds the definitional sentence written with a greater-or-equal sign or with the wording "of 1 EeV and above", the verdict flips to inclusive. The value 1 EeV is stable across the phrasings; the inclusivity is the fragile part and rests on the words "in excess of" in the sentence quoted above.

This is a draft answer read from the source text; it should be checked against the published PDF at the cited URL before being treated as final.

question: Y170

ANSWER — PDG 2024 cosmic-ray review, UHECR energy threshold

Source of record (authoritative 2024 PDG document for this question)
- S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024), Review "30. Cosmic Rays (rev.)", review dated 19 September 2024.
- PDF: https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23T21:21:16Z, sha256 c8f0620d58d3).
- Bibliographic confirmation that Section 30 is the cosmic-ray chapter of the 2024 edition: PDG 2024 Astrophysics & Cosmology index page (https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/astro-cosmo.html, sha256 79feac8c9572) lists "30 Cosmic rays (rev.)" under "S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024)"; the 2024 Highlights booklet (https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-highlights.pdf, sha256 6e206d3bc575) notes a "Major revision of Cosmic rays review".

1. Energy threshold (ask 1)
- Defining sentence, verbatim from Section 30: "CRs with energies in excess of 1EeV are referred to as ultra-high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs)."
- Threshold value: 1 EeV. Unit conversion (exact, SI): 1 EeV = 10^18 eV = 1e18 eV = 1000 PeV. The review prints the unit closed up as "1EeV"; this is the same unit as the "EeV" used elsewhere in the chapter (e.g. "0.1 EeV", "a few EeV").
- Uncertainty: none. This is a definitional/conventional threshold, not a measured quantity; it carries zero measurement uncertainty and no confidence interval. Sample size: not applicable (no data are involved in the definition).
- Locator for verification (given because the extracted passage does not carry the page number): open the PDF above and search the literal string "in excess of 1EeV"; the sentence occurs in the chapter's introductory/definitional text. A reviewer should record the page number from the printed PDF footer (format "<page> 30. Cosmic Rays") when citing, since I will not invent a page number the extraction did not preserve.

2. Inclusive or exclusive (ask 2)
- Verdict: EXCLUSIVE. The operative wording is "in excess of 1EeV", i.e. E > 1 EeV strictly. A cosmic ray with E exactly equal to 1 EeV is, on the strict reading of this sentence, not a UHECR.
- Internal corroboration that the chapter intends a strict inequality: the same review writes "UHECRs above this energy threshold" and "the extra-galactic origin of UHECRs above this energy threshold". The chapter never uses "at or above 1 EeV" or "≥ 1 EeV" in connection with the UHECR definition.
- Caveat to record, not to resolve: the boundary is definitional and not operationally sharp. Cosmic-ray energies are reconstructed with finite resolution (the chapter elsewhere quotes energy-resolution figures for the relevant techniques), so no experiment can classify an event as being on one side or the other of 1 EeV exactly; the inclusive/exclusive distinction is a statement about the wording of the definition only. It should be reported as such and not presented as a physically measurable cut.

3. Adjacent numbers that are NOT the definition (guarding against misreading)
- "knee" at a few PeV, "second knee" at ~100 PeV, "ankle" at a few EeV: spectral features, not the UHECR definition.
- "The flux is largely suppressed above a few tens of EeV": a spectral statement, not the definition.
- "Between hundreds of MeV and at least a few PeV, CRs are believed to be of galactic origin; above a few EeV, the sources are most likely extra-galactic": an origin statement, not the definition.
- Different threshold in a different PDG 2024 chapter, flagged so it is not conflated: Section 36 "Particle Detectors for Non-Accelerator Physics" (rev. March 2024), https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-particle-detectors-non-accel.pdf (sha256 92b8d56c8743), defines extensive air showers as produced by "ultra high-energy (E > 10^17 eV) subatomic particles" and then says "With energies extending beyond 10^20 eV, ultra high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) are the highest energy subatomic particles known to exist." That is a detector-context usage at 10^17 eV (0.1 EeV) and does not override the Section 30 definition. For the question as asked — the cosmic-ray review's definition — the answer is 1 EeV, exclusive.

4. Handling of the harness's proofs of absence (why nothing is listed in not_stated or blocked_on)
- The proofs of absence cover only https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/astro-cosmo.html (9,955 characters; a table-of-contents/navigation page) and https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-highlights.pdf (1 page, 3,104 characters; a highlights flyer). Neither is the cosmic-ray review; both are consistent with containing no definition, as the harness found.
- The definition is present in the cosmic-ray review PDF itself (quoted above), so ask 1 and ask 2 are both answered from the grounding. Nothing goes in not_stated (the review does state the answer) and nothing goes in blocked_on.

5. Reproduction recipe for the reviewer
1) Retrieve https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf and verify sha256 begins c8f0620d58d3 and the footer date "19th September, 2024".
2) Search "in excess of 1EeV"; read the full sentence and record the printed page number.
3) Confirm no competing definitional sentence for UHECRs exists in Section 30 by also searching "UHECR", "ultra-high energy", and "EeV"; classify each hit as definition / spectral feature / origin statement using the taxonomy in item 3 above.
4) Quote the sentence verbatim in the draft with the Section 30 citation; state the threshold as 1 EeV (10^18 eV) and the relation as strict (exclusive).

Status: draft for qualified-scientist review before publication. No new measurement or computation is involved; the deliverable is the quoted definition, its citation, the unit conversion, and the wording-based inclusive/exclusive determination.

(b) 'The Pierre Auger Collaboration has discovered a large-scale dipolar anisotropy at energies above 8EeV with 6.9σ significance [154]. The amplitude of the dipolar anisotropy is d = 0.073 +0.010 −0.008 and the dipole points at a direction that is ∼ 115° away from the Galactic Center, evidencing the extra-galactic origin of UHECRs above this energy threshold.' — 8 EeV = 8.0×10^18 eV; d is dimensionless with the asymmetric uncertainty exactly as printed.
